stem: A urine culture from a stable client with uncomplicated cystitis grows ESBL-producing Escherichia coli susceptible to both nitrofurantoin and meropenem. Which stewardship principle should the nurse recognize when reviewing the treatment plan?

options.A: Nitrofurantoin is a preferred option; although carbapenems can be effective, avoiding them when an effective narrower option is available helps preserve their activity for infections with fewer treatment choices.
options.B: Meropenem should be preferred whenever an ESBL-producing organism is identified, regardless of infection site or susceptibility to other recommended agents.
options.C: Carbapenems have no activity against ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, so meropenem susceptibility should be considered a laboratory error.
options.D: Once ESBL production is identified, antimicrobial susceptibility results no longer influence antibiotic selection.

rationale: A is correct. Current IDSA 2026 antimicrobial-resistance guidance lists nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as preferred options for uncomplicated cystitis caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales when active. Carbapenems can be effective alternatives, but their use is discouraged when an effective preferred option is available because limiting carbapenem use preserves their activity for future infections in which treatment options may be more restricted. B overgeneralizes carbapenem use without considering infection site and other susceptible agents. C is false because ESBL-producing Enterobacterales generally remain susceptible to carbapenems. D is incorrect because the IDSA guidance assumes in-vitro activity of selected agents and repeatedly uses susceptibility results to guide therapy.
educational_objective: Apply antimicrobial stewardship by using infection site and susceptibility data to select an effective preferred agent and conserving carbapenems when narrower recommended therapy is active, rather than treating ESBL status alone as an automatic indication for meropenem.
source_organization: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA); U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
source_document_title: IDSA 2026 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial Resistant Gram-Negative Infections; Meropenem for Injection Prescribing Information
source_version_date: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance published July 27, 2026; DailyMed meropenem label updated November 14, 2025; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance — Section 1, ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, Question 1.1: nitrofurantoin and TMP-SMX are preferred for uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis; fluoroquinolones and carbapenems are effective alternatives but their use is discouraged when preferred agents are active because limiting them preserves activity for future infections. Section 1 introduction: ESBL-E generally remain susceptible to carbapenems and treatment suggestions assume in-vitro activity. DailyMed Meropenem — Section 1 Usage: use for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria.
source_claim_supported: For uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis with nitrofurantoin susceptibility, nitrofurantoin is preferred and carbapenem use should generally be conserved; ESBL status does not replace infection-site and susceptibility-guided antimicrobial selection.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply medication knowledge to safe antimicrobial therapy, evaluate medication effectiveness, and support appropriate medication use.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antimicrobial stewardship and carbapenem conservation
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw 'carbapenems are last-line broad-spectrum drugs' generalization into a site- and susceptibility-specific stewardship decision using the newly current July 2026 IDSA AMR guidance. The final item avoids labeling carbapenems universally as 'last-line' and tests when conserving meropenem is actually recommended.

audit_findings.clinical_category: antimicrobial stewardship / ESBL cystitis / carbapenem conservation
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against the current IDSA 2026 AMR guidance published July 27, 2026 and a current DailyMed meropenem label. The answer is tied to uncomplicated cystitis and demonstrated susceptibility rather than a generic hierarchy of antibiotic strength.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A exactly matches IDSA's preferred-option and conservation rationale. B ignores infection site and other susceptible preferred agents. C contradicts IDSA's statement that ESBL-E generally remain carbapenem-susceptible. D contradicts susceptibility-based recommendations throughout the guidance.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it applies the current site-specific stewardship recommendation.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible over-escalation error; carbapenem therapy is not automatically preferred for every ESBL infection.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; carbapenems commonly retain activity against ESBL-E.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; susceptibility data remain central to antibiotic selection.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The stem specifies uncomplicated cystitis, clinical stability, and susceptibility to nitrofurantoin and meropenem. Under current IDSA guidance these details make A uniquely correct.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address ESBL treatment and stewardship; none is an unrelated mechanism or administration detail.
audit_findings.blueprint: The item tests safe and appropriate pharmacologic selection and stewardship principles under Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the July 2026 update rather than relying on 2024 guidance. Challenged whether meropenem could still be chosen because it is active; IDSA explicitly discourages carbapenem use for uncomplicated ESBL cystitis when nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX is active. No unsupported universal 'last-line' language remains.
